← Flood monitoring





Flood fusion: analysis and results
Checkpoint 2026-10-21, exported from the review doc (https://claude.ai/artifact/EzpeTJ8mnRVPaw6rAE7Xop) by scripts/fusion/doc_to_book.py. The doc is where the analysis is developed; this book is the record. Every number comes from a file under results/; log.md lists the command behind each one.
2026-10-15 · Zack Arno
Flood fusion combines GFM (radar), FloodScan and GFDS (microwave) and VIIRS (optical) into one daily probability of flooding on a 0.01° grid. This page sets out how it is tested and what the test found: scope, inputs, how each cell is classified, how scoring works, how events are split for testing, and the results. All 170 usable flood events in Africa, Asia, South America and Oceania are each scored once, by a model fitted only on events in other river basins. Every term is defined in the Glossary tab. docs/methods.md in the repo describes the same mechanics with the code that does each step, and docs/log.md is the ledger: every step so far in order, with the command that reproduces it, its output files and its commit.

title: 2  The basics: what is classified, and how it is scored
text:
2.1 From pixels to cells: how every layer lands on one grid
The unit is one cell on one day. A cell is a 0.01° square, about 1.1 km across. For every cell on every day, each satellite product says one of three things: flood, dry, or couldn’t see. Fusion turns the three products’ reports into a probability P, and calls the cell flooded when P ≥ 0.5. A gold map, on the day it was made, labels each cell it examined flooded or dry; cells it did not examine have no label.
Only labelled cells on map days are scored. A map day is a day with a gold map. Scoring compares the product’s call with the gold label, cell by cell, on those days only:
Cell level: counts, summed. Hits, misses and false alarms are counted over every labelled cell, every map day and every event, then:
Event level: one verdict per event. An event is caught if, on some day from 3 days before its first map to 3 days after its last, the product flags at least 10% of the cells gold flooded (and at least 5). It is a false event if the same rule fires on days 30 to 10 before the first map, when no flood was mapped. Both are reported as shares of the 148 events with at least 5 flooded cells. Here every event counts once, whatever its size.
Which days are used for what:
Two rates that come up often, with their denominators:
Why the gap between them matters. Precision depends on how common flood is where you score. With the same false-alarm rate, a flood 60 times rarer gives far lower precision. Every precision on this page is from map days inside mapped floods; precision on ordinary days has not been measured yet (Next steps, 6).
Nothing is compared at a product’s own resolution. Every layer, from 20 m radar to 9 km microwave, is first put onto the same grid of 0.01° cells (about 1.1 km). “Pixel” always means a product’s own native pixel; “cell” always means our grid square. The rules below are the whole resampling; each lives in configs/fusion.yaml under the key shown.
Why the same 50% and 30% everywhere. Half observed before a cell counts as seen, and 30% flooded before it counts as flood, are applied to every product and to gold alike, so no product is held to a different standard than the answer key. The cost is that a flood covering less than 30% of a cell is invisible to everyone, gold included.
What this means for the coarse products. One FloodScan or GFDS pixel sets about 81 of our cells at once, so their hits and false alarms come in 9 km blocks (visible as squares in the maps in this book). They are scored cell by cell like everything else, which is fair to them where a flood is large and harsh where it is narrow.
Days. Every layer is daily except the static ones (HAND, permanent water, land type: fixed) and normally wet (one map per calendar month). A product that has no file for a day gives “couldn’t see” on every cell, never dry.

title: 3  How the pieces fit together
text:
← Flood monitoring





Inputs. Three kinds of satellite product give each 0.01° cell, each day, a value: flood, dry or “couldn’t see” (Inputs).
Fixed layers. Elevation, permanent water and land cover decide which cells can flood, and whether each is open, vegetated or urban (Grid, domain and strata).
Gold labels. Expert flood maps label each examined cell flooded, dry or none on their map days. The 30 days before and 60 days after each event add dry labels (Gold labels; Events, days and how counts add up).
Fitting. For each source and land type, the events used for fitting give two numbers: how often it says flood where gold says flooded (hit rate), and where gold says dry (false-alarm rate).
Fusion. Each day, fusion turns the sources’ reports into a probability of flooding using those rates. P ≥ 0.5 counts as a flood call (How fusion and scoring work).
Scoring. Fusion and each product are compared with gold cell by cell, on the map days of events not used for fitting. The counts are summed into recall, precision and F1, and per event into “caught or not” (Testing; From counts to totals; Was the event caught?).

The project plan judges fusion on three criteria:

(a) coverage: a value on more floodable cells each day than any single product;
(b) mapping skill: in each land type, CSI at least that of the best single product;
(c) reliability: its probabilities mean what they say. Of cells given P 0.6, about 60% should be flooded; the slope between predicted and observed must be 0.8–1.2.

title: 4  Scope and events
text:
← Flood monitoring




170 flood events are in scope, in Africa, Asia, South America and Oceania. Europe and North America are set aside for now.
An event is one activation code in a gold catalog. Each of its gold maps covers an area on one date. Areas within 0.05° of each other are merged into one window, and every window covers every day from 30 days before the event’s first map to 60 days after its last.
An event is built once its data is prepared. For each window and each of its 91 or more days, the gold labels and every source’s flood, dry or “couldn’t see” value are put on the 0.01° grid. The result is saved as one file per window (an event cube). Fitting and scoring read only these files, which is why re-running them is cheap and building new events is not.

From pixels to cells. Each product pixel goes to the cell that holds its centre. A cell is “couldn’t see” if fewer than half its pixels were observed that day. Otherwise it is flood if at least 30% of the observed pixels are flood, and dry if not. FloodScan and GFDS pixels are larger than a cell (about 9 km), so every cell copies the value of the 9 km pixel it sits in.
Why the sources have gaps.

GFM: Sentinel-1 passes over a given place only every 6 to 12 days, so GFM has no image on most days.
VIIRS: it sees reflected sunlight like a camera, so cloud blocks it, and floods come with cloud.
Passive microwave (FloodScan, GFDS): it measures the energy the ground itself gives off. It sees through cloud every day, but only at about 9 km.

The in-cell rules (at least half observed, at least 30% flood) are the same for every source and for gold. A river that floods 10% of a cell is therefore dry everywhere. MODIS was tested only as an experiment; see Other approaches tried. FloodScan is used under AER’s commercial licence, and whether it covers the non-Africa regions is still to be confirmed.

title: 7  Grid, domain and strata

← Flood monitoring




Every cell gets three fixed attributes before any satellite data is read: whether it can flood (the domain), its land type (the stratum), and, through its event, a continent and a river basin. Only the land type changes the model. Continent and basin are used for scope, for building the test folds and for reporting.
Land type matters because each source’s accuracy depends on what covers the ground. Radar and optical sensors cannot see water under trees, and buildings confuse radar. So the model learns its hit and false-alarm rates separately for open, vegetated and urban cells. Each group of cells with one land type is a stratum.

title: 8  Water versus flood
text:
← Flood monitoring




Every product here detects water. A flood is water that is not normally there. Deciding what counts as normal is a separate step, done after the water is detected, and each product does it its own way. The gold maps make that call too, by eye. This section shows where they differ and what that does to the scores.



Who counts which water as flood · three kinds of water; the gold maps, four products and fusion


Three kinds of water.

Permanent water: river channels and lakes, water nearly all the time (JRC Global Surface Water occurrence of at least 90%). Every product and the gold maps leave it out of “flood”, and cells that are mostly permanent water are removed from the domain.
Normally wet this month: water that is usually there at this time of year: a wet-season floodplain, a wetland, a flooded rice paddy. A cell is normally wet in a month if at least 30% of its 30 m pixels were water in that calendar month in at least half the years from 1984 to 2021 (JRC monthly recurrence). This is where the products and gold disagree.
Unusual water: water that is not normally there this month. This is the flood everyone agrees on.

How each draws the line on normally-wet cells.

GFM subtracts its own reference water, so it reports only unusual water.
GFDS compares each day’s signal with its long-term mean, so wet-season water reads as above normal and counts as flood.
VIIRS and FloodScan appear to count seasonal water as flood; this is not confirmed.
The gold maps are split. On map days, of the labelled cells that are normally wet, 52% are labelled flooded and 48% dry. These cells are only 7% of the labelled cells, but hold 38% of the gold flood. One map can do both, as in the example below: the analyst left the main river channel out of the flood but counted a large seasonal wetland as flooded.




Bangladesh, 22 August 2017: normally-wet cells, the gold map, fusion’s flood calls, and how each call is scored


How to read it. Bangladesh, 22 August 2017 (FL20170815BGD), one of the four Bangladesh floods that hold 40% of the gold flood. Fusion here is the cross-validated model, fitted without this event.

A: cells normally wet in August. The Jamuna river and its side channels run north to south; the large area in the east is a seasonal wetland.
B: the gold map. Inside the satellite footprint (the tilted rectangle) the analyst marked flooded cells (blue) and dry cells (sand). The river channel is mostly marked dry: the analyst left it out of the flood, presumably as normal water. The eastern wetland is marked flooded.
C: fusion’s flood calls. The square blocks are the microwave products’ 9 km cells.
D: how each of fusion’s calls is scored. Green: a hit. Orange: fusion says flood on a cell gold calls dry but that is normally wet, mostly the river channel. Red: fusion says flood on a gold-dry cell that is normally dry, mostly the edges of the coarse microwave blocks. Grey: flood fusion missed.

Is orange a false alarm? Only if the target is flood. Fusion saw water there, and on a cell that is normally wet this month the water is probably really there; gold left it out of the flood, most likely as normal water. The scores count it as a false alarm because gold says dry. A product that reports water, and leaves “is this normal?” to a later, explicit step, is not wrong; that is the water-first design at the end of this section.
How much this changes the scores. Over all 170 events, on map days:

fusion makes 202,714 flood calls on gold-dry cells, and 39,076 of them (19%) are on normally-wet cells, the orange kind;
not counting those, fusion’s precision would be 0.51 instead of 0.46;
the other 81%, the red kind, are on cells that are normally dry. They are coarse microwave cells reaching past the flood edge, water the analysts did not map, water the JRC record misses (it cannot see through persistent cloud), or plain errors. These labels cannot tell them apart.

Removing normal water after the fact does not work with these labels. If fusion dropped every flood call on a normally-wet cell, as one more post-processing step, it would remove the 39,076 calls gold labels dry but also 82,037 calls gold labels flooded. Recall would fall from 0.43 to 0.22, precision from 0.46 to 0.36, and F1 from 0.44 to 0.27. Every single product lost the same way in the first run (VIIRS recall 0.41 to 0.35, microwave 0.47 to 0.39). The reason is that gold counts about half of that water as flood: a masked product cannot be scored fairly against unmasked gold. GFM’s recall (all cells) is lower on normally-wet cells than elsewhere (0.11 against 0.16); whether that is its stricter definition or less coverage there has not been separated.
A second example, where little of the flood is normally wet:



Water versus flood on one day: gold map, normally-wet water in August, and GFM, VIIRS and FloodScan, Punjab, Pakistan, 28 August 2025


How to read it. Punjab, Pakistan, 28 August 2025 (EMSR838, one window).

Gold maps 1,152 flooded cells along the river. Only 11% of them are normally wet in August: the river channel itself (top middle).
GFM could not see a large patch (grey), which counts against its recall here (0.62, all cells). Where it saw, nearly every flood call was right: precision 0.97.
VIIRS caught almost all of the mapped flood (recall 0.95). It also flagged water outside it (precision 0.63), some of which may be real water the analysts did not map.
FloodScan’s 9 km cells catch the flood only in coarse blocks: recall 0.37, precision 0.58.

Scores are for this one day, on gold-labelled cells.
A cleaner design: detect water, then remove normal water once.



Where the normal-water step happens · today and water-first


Today each product removes normal water its own way before fusion sees it, so fusion mixes several definitions, and gold mixes them again. In a water-first design, each product gives fusion its water; fusion estimates the chance of water; and one normal-water baseline turns that into a chance of flood. The definition of flood becomes one setting that users can see and change. It would make the target clear. It would not by itself fix the over-confident probabilities, which persist on both kinds of cell (Results, Water versus flood: where the problems sit).

title: 9  Gold labels
text:
← Flood monitoring




A gold map gives each cell it examined one label for its map date: flooded, dry or none. Cells it did not examine are never scored.
Each map has two parts: the flood polygons and the area the analyst examined. Both are drawn onto a 0.001° grid, so each 0.01° cell holds 10 × 10 = 100 sub-pixels.







label
rule




flooded
at least half the cell was examined, and at least 30% of the examined part is flood


dry
at least half examined, under 30% flood, and under 30% “flood possible”


none
under half examined; or examined, under 30% flood and at least 30% “flood possible”



Maps of the same event on the same day are merged, and flood wins over dry.
Where the thresholds come from. The 30% flood share and the at-least-half rule are the same for gold and for every product, so a cell is “flooded” by one definition on both sides. As a result, a flood covering under 30% of a cell is invisible to scoring (see Not yet validated). These thresholds, the 30-day and 60-day periods, the 10% daily fading and the P ≥ 0.5 cut-off were all set in the project plan before any result was seen. None is tuned to the results.

9.0.1 The days before and after each event
Gold maps exist only on flood days. To learn how often each source raises a false alarm on ordinary days, the model also needs dry labels away from the flood. These come from the 30 days before an event’s first map and the 60 days after its last.

In those days, every cell the maps examined is labelled dry,
except cells that were flooded on any map day in their window. Those get no label, because floodwater takes weeks to drain. In open land in the first run (D-39), fusion still called flood on 48% of days 1–30 after the event in those cells, against 5% in cells that never flooded. This rule was decided on 14 October (ADR 0006); the old rule’s scores are shown alongside.

These days are used to fit the false-alarm rates and to check reliability. Recall, precision and F1 are scored on gold-map days only.
What the labels cannot tell us. Analysts map what they saw; unmapped water inside the examined area counts as dry. Many Copernicus maps are drawn from Sentinel-1, the same satellite as GFM, which favours GFM. Results are therefore also reported for the events whose maps are not from Sentinel-1.

title: 10  How fusion and scoring work
text:
← Flood monitoring





10.0.1 Fusion’s probability
For each cell and day, fusion adds up evidence from the sources that observed it:

a source saying flood raises the odds by its hit rate divided by its false-alarm rate, in that land type;
a source saying dry lowers them by its miss rate (1 − hit rate) divided by its correct-dry rate (1 − false-alarm rate);
couldn’t see adds nothing.

Odds, with an example. Odds are P / (1 − P); a probability of 0.002 is odds of about 1 to 500. In open land, in the first run, the base flood rate is 0.16%, and VIIRS’s hit rate is 0.66 with a false-alarm rate of 5.5%. One VIIRS flood report multiplies the odds by 0.66 / 0.055 = 12, which lifts P from 0.0016 to about 0.02. Reaching 0.5 takes several sources agreeing, or several days in a row.
Yesterday’s value carries over, fading 10% a day back towards the base flood rate for that land type. The base rate comes from the global random sample: how often GFM sees flood on an ordinary day. Fusion counts as flood when P ≥ 0.5. The hit and false-alarm rates are fitted only on the events in the other four folds (see Testing).
Fitting is counting. For each source and land type, two shares are counted on the events used for fitting:

hit rate: of the gold-flooded cells the source observed, the share it called flood;
false-alarm rate: of the gold-dry cells it observed, the share it called flood.

docs/methods.md calls these sensitivity and 1 − specificity. Half a hit is added to each count and one to each total, so no rate is ever exactly 0 or 1. The daily fading works on the log of the odds, not on P.

Recall = hits ÷ (hits + misses): the share of gold-flooded cells the product flags.
Precision = hits ÷ (hits + false alarms): the share of its flood calls that gold confirms.
F1 = 2 × hits ÷ (2 × hits + misses + false alarms): the balance of recall and precision, high only when both are. It is the headline single score.
CSI = hits ÷ (hits + misses + false alarms): of all cells the product or gold calls flooded, the share where both do. It ranks products the same as F1 and appears only where criterion (b) needs it.

A worked example. One gold day, 100 labelled cells, 30 of them flooded. A product flags 25 cells, 20 of them among the 30 flooded. That is 20 hits, 5 false alarms, 10 misses and 65 correct dry: recall 0.67, precision 0.80, F1 0.73.


10.0.3 Two views, and how totals are formed

All cells answers “what does a user get on a given day?”. A cell the product couldn’t see counts against it as a miss, which lowers recall but never precision.
Observed cells answers “how good is the product when it looks?”. It scores only the cells a product saw, and fusion is scored on the same cells for a fair comparison.
Totals are formed as described in From counts to totals: large floods weigh more, so every score is also reported per continent and per land type.

Precision here is measured inside mapped flood areas on flood days, where about a tenth of labelled cells on map days are flooded (12% in open land). On ordinary days far fewer are, so precision there is much lower. Measuring it needs non-event data: the global random sample, with GFM as stand-in truth. The event-level false-event check below covers part of this.

title: 11  Testing: five folds by river basin
text:
← Flood monitoring




Every event is tested once, by a model fitted without it. A model scored on the events it was fitted on looks better than it is, because it has already seen them. The events are split into five folds. For each fold, the hit and false-alarm rates are fitted on the other four folds, and the fold’s events are scored. The scores are then pooled over all five folds.

Whole river basins stay in one fold (HydroBASINS level 4), so a neighbouring flood on the same river never helps score its neighbour.
Folds are balanced on flooded area first: the basins with the most gold flood are spread across folds, then the rest are placed to even out each continent’s events. A basin cannot be split, and one dominates: four UNOSAT floods in Bangladesh (2017, 2018, 2020 and 2022) share one HydroBASINS level-4 basin and hold 40% of all gold flooded cell-days. Their fold holds 43% of the open-land flood and 62% of the vegetated flood; each other fold holds 8–17%. When that fold is scored, its rates are fitted on the remaining 57% of the open-land flood and 38% of the vegetated flood.
It is cheap. Fitting is counting, so five fits cost little. Scoring all events once took about two minutes on the laptop, under both rules for the days before and after.
Anything tuned is tuned inside each fold, never on the fold being scored.

title: 12  From counts to totals
text:
← Flood monitoring




Every score on this page is built from the same counts, in these steps:

One count per labelled cell, per day, per product: hit, miss, false alarm or correct dry. Every product, and fusion, is scored on the same labelled cells.
Per event. Counts are summed over each window’s cells and days, then over the event’s windows, and kept per event, land type and kind of day. Every number below is a sum of these.
Fitting, per fold. The counts of the four folds not being scored, per land type, give each source’s hit rate (map days, the only days with flood labels) and false-alarm rate (map days plus every day before and after), counted on floodable cells only, where fusion makes its calls.
Scoring. Each fold’s events are scored with the rates fitted on the other four folds. The map-day counts of all 170 events, each tested once, are summed, and recall, precision and F1 are computed from the sums: overall, per continent, per land type and per product.
Pooled, not averaged. A large flood has more cell-days, so it weighs more; five events hold 47% of all gold flooded cell-days, and one basin’s four Bangladesh floods 40% (named under Testing). That is why results are also shown per continent and land type, with intervals from resampling whole events (a bootstrap: the scores are recomputed on many random re-draws of the events, and their spread shows how much they depend on which events happened to be mapped).
Event level. One yes or no per event (caught or not) and one number (days to detection), reported as shares of events. There every event counts equally.

14.0.3 Can fusion beat the cascade? Three switches
Fusion differs from the cascade in three ways. Each was switched on and off separately, which gives 2 × 2 × 2 versions of fusion (scripts/fusion/cv_pattern_model.py; the rules and the test for success were committed before it ran):

How evidence is combined. As built, each product’s report adds its own evidence, as if the products were independent. The alternative learns, on the training folds, how strongly each combination of reports signals flood: 27 combinations of flood, dry or couldn’t see, per land type. “Couldn’t see” itself carries no evidence, because cloud and flood come together on map days, and that would not carry over to ordinary days.
Memory. As built, yesterday’s belief carries over (decay 0.9), so evidence builds up over days. The alternative judges each day on its own, like the cascade.
Threshold. As built, a cell is called flooded at P ≥ 0.5. The alternative uses the threshold with the best F1 on the training folds, chosen inside each fold.

The test for success was fixed beforehand: above the cascade on both pooled and basin-weighted F1, with fewer false events.
In the first run the threshold could go down to 0.02. 15.0.1 CYGNSS: a first look at a fourth source
CYGNSS is a NASA constellation that measures GPS signals reflected off the ground; calm water reflects strongly. The UC Berkeley daily watermask built from it gives water, land or no data on a 0.01° grid, from August 2018, between latitudes 37.4° S and 37.4° N, a few days behind real time. Like the microwave products it sees through cloud, but at 1 km instead of 9 km. 148 of the 170 events, holding 82% of the gold flood, fall inside its dates and latitudes. It is read with your Earthdata token, fetching only the rows each window needs: about 11 MB a day for the largest window, instead of a 257 MB file.
Checked before scoring:

It is not a daily snapshot. Over a Bangladesh window in July–August 2020, 6% of cells change from one day to the next, 13% over 8 days and 24% over 30 days, and the files’ own metadata gives a 31-day coverage. It behaves like a rolling composite of several weeks. So it cannot enter fusion as fresh daily evidence: fusion’s memory would count the same water many times.
Its cells are offset by half a cell from ours, so each of our cells takes a quarter of four CYGNSS cells. A cell is observed if at least half of it has data, and water if at least 30% of the observed part is water, the rules every source uses.

title: 17  Next steps
text:
← Flood monitoring




Steps 1–4 are done (15 October). Steps 5–7 extend the analysis, and each waits on something outside this work.

1. Settle the two proposals: the rule for days before and after each event, and the event-level rules (the 10% share, the ±3-day window, the ordinary-day period). Decided for you on 14 October, before any result existed (ADRs 0006 and 0007).
2. Code changes, each with its test and a short decision record (ADR), and docs/methods.md updated in the same commit:

scope and event selection in configs/fusion.yaml (continents listed, no quotas or size limits)
three land types instead of six strata
the days-before-and-after rule
five folds by basin, balanced on flood area

3. Build the 51 new events. All built (15 October).
4. Re-run fitting and scoring over the five folds on all 170 events: cell-level (all cells and observed cells, per continent and land type) and event-level. Done (15 October): results/cv/ in the repo, Results above, and docs/final_report.md.
5. MODIS in the optical vote. The stake: where VIIRS has files it adds 0.08 F1 to fusion, and the VIIRS gap holds 28% of the gold flood. Needs MODIS over every event window, a Databricks job. It is blocked on an Earthdata login the job can use: either your personal token stored as a Databricks secret, or the team account fixed.
6. Precision on ordinary days from the global random sample, with the deferred check for false events away from floods (ADR 0007).
7. Gauge test: choose a gauge source inside the four continents.
8. Normally-wet stratum. Fit each source’s rates separately for cells normally wet in that calendar month (JRC monthly recurrence), within each land type. False-alarm rates differ 3 to 11 times between the two (Results, Water versus flood). Cheap: the masks are cached for every map-day month; the other months of the 51 new events need about 195 more window-month downloads (minutes). It is not expected to fix the flat probabilities, which persist within both kinds of cell.
9. Beat the cascade. Fusion as built only matches “VIIRS, else GFM, else microwave” on the reference score and loses to it basin-weighted. The direct test is to learn the evidence for each combination of reports (each of the 27 patterns of flood, dry or couldn’t see from the three sources, per land type) on the training folds, instead of multiplying each source’s evidence as if they were independent. This changes fixed decision 7 of the original brief, so it needs your yes. Success: above the cascade on the pooled and the basin-weighted scores, while keeping fusion’s lower false-event rate. Done 16 October: no version passes (Results, Can fusion beat the cascade?).
10. Choose the operating point: catch floods or avoid false alarms. Step 9 found (16 October) that no version beats the cascade on both F1 and false events. Fusion as built sits at one end (F1 0.44, false events on 34% of events); the cascade and the no-memory versions at the other (F1 0.46–0.49, false events 64%). Which end, or a point between, depends on how the product will be used: an alert that must not cry wolf, or a map that must not miss water. The points in between are now shown (Results, The trade-off, threshold by threshold); the choice is yours.
11. CYGNSS on all events in its coverage. On 8 events it has the best F1 of any single product (0.47) and the highest recall (0.67), but low precision on ordinary cells (Other approaches tried, CYGNSS). Score it on all 148 events inside its dates and latitudes, with intervals, as a slowly updating layer: about 590 map days, read by window with your Earthdata token, an hour or two of downloads.

title: Appendix A — Glossary

A.1 Events and gold maps
Every term the analysis uses, in plain words, grouped by topic.

title: Appendix A — Glossary
text:
term
meaning




gold map
an expert-drawn flood map from Copernicus EMS or UNOSAT, used as the reference answer


activation code
the ID a mapping service gives one flood response, e.g. EMSR838. One code is one event


examined area
the part of a gold map the analyst actually looked at. Outside it there is no label, flooded or dry


map day
a date on which an event, or one of its windows, has a gold map. A window is scored only on its own map days


event period
from an event’s first map day to its last


window
one area of an event, processed on its own. Maps within 0.05° of each other share a window. A window covers 30 days before the event period to 60 days after it


days before and after
the 30 days before the first map and the 60 after the last. Examined cells are labelled dry there, to measure false alarms on ordinary days, except cells flooded on a map day of their window, which get no label there


built
an event whose gold labels and source values have been prepared on the grid and saved (an event cube per window)

title: Appendix A — Glossary
text:
A.2 Grid and cells







term
meaning




cell
one 0.01° × 0.01° square of the grid, about 1.1 km across at the equator


cell-day
one cell on one day: the unit every count is made of. A window-day is one window on one day


sub-pixel
one of the 100 squares of 0.001° a gold map is drawn onto inside each cell


HAND
height above nearest drainage: how far a point sits above the nearest stream. From the GLO-30 elevation model


floodable
at least 30% of the cell lies less than 15 m above the nearest stream


permanent water
water at least 90% of the time over 1984–2021 (JRC Global Surface Water). Cells that are mostly permanent water are removed


domain
floodable cells that are not permanent water. Nothing outside it is predicted or scored


normally wet
a cell where at least 30% of the 30 m pixels were water in that calendar month in at least half of the years observed (JRC monthly recurrence, 1984–2021): a wet-season floodplain, wetland or rice paddy


reference water
a map of the water that is normally there, which a product or an analyst leaves out of “flood”. GFM uses its own; the gold analysts decide by eye, and do not always decide the same way


unusual water
water that is not normally there in that month: the flood every source agrees on


water-first design
a proposal: fuse the products’ water, then turn it into flood with one normal-water baseline, so the definition of flood is one visible setting


land type, stratum
open, vegetated or urban, from ESA WorldCover. A stratum is the group of cells with one land type; the model’s rates are fitted per stratum


snow season
a month in which a cell is usually snow-covered (ERA5-Land). Not used: almost all snow-season gold flood is in Europe, which is out of scope

title: Appendix A — Glossary
text:
A.3 Satellites and sources







term
meaning




radar (SAR)
the satellite sends a microwave pulse and reads the echo; calm water reflects it away and looks dark. Works through cloud and at night, but cannot see water under trees


Sentinel-1, GFM
the European radar satellites, and Copernicus’s Global Flood Monitoring product made from them. A given place gets an image only every 6 to 12 days


optical
sees reflected sunlight, like a camera. Blocked by cloud


VIIRS, MODIS
US optical sensors that image the whole Earth daily; NOAA and NASA make flood maps from them


passive microwave
measures the energy the ground itself gives off; wet ground gives off less. Sees through cloud every day, but only at about 9 km


FloodScan, SFED
AER’s product from passive microwave; SFED is the share of each 9 km cell that is flooded


GFDS
JRC/GDACS Global Flood Detection System, also passive microwave, about 9 km


couldn’t see
the product had no usable observation for that cell that day (also called NoData). Never counted as dry


microwave vote
FloodScan and GFDS combined: flood if either says flood, dry if at least one observed and neither says flood


optical vote
the same for VIIRS and MODIS (proposed)


CYGNSS
a NASA constellation measuring GPS signals reflected off the ground; the UC Berkeley daily watermask made from it is a rolling multi-week composite of surface water at 0.01°, within 37.4° of the equator, from August 2018

title: Appendix A — Glossary
text:
A.4 Fusion







term
meaning




hit rate
for one source and land type: the share of gold-flooded cells it observed that it called flood (docs/methods.md: sensitivity)


false-alarm rate
the share of gold-dry cells it observed that it called flood (1 − specificity)


fitting
counting hits, misses, false alarms and correct dries on the events used for fitting, to get those two rates


base flood rate (prior)
how often a cell of that land type is flooded on an ordinary day, from the global random sample’s 30 blocks in the four continents: about 0.23% in open land, 0.01% in vegetated and 0.005% in urban land


odds
P / (1 − P). P 0.002 is odds of about 1 to 500. Fusion multiplies the odds by each source’s hit rate over its false-alarm rate


log-odds
the logarithm of the odds; fusion adds evidence and fades yesterday’s value on this scale


P
fusion’s probability that a cell is flooded that day; P ≥ 0.5 counts as a flood call


memory
yesterday’s log-odds carry over at 0.9 of their distance from the base rate, so evidence builds up over days


cascade
a baseline that needs no fitting: for each cell-day, the first product that observed it, in the order VIIRS, GFM, microwave vote

title: Appendix A — Glossary
text:
A.5 Scoring and testing







term
meaning




hit, miss, false alarm, correct dry
product flood where gold is flooded; product dry (or couldn’t see) where gold is flooded; product flood where gold is dry; product dry where gold is dry


recall
the share of gold-flooded cells a product flags


precision
the share of a product’s flood calls that gold confirms


F1
the balance of recall and precision (their harmonic mean); high only when both are. The headline score


CSI
hits ÷ (hits + misses + false alarms); ranks products the same as F1. Used only for criterion (b)


all cells, observed cells
two scoring views: a product’s gaps count as misses / only the cells it saw are scored


pooled
counts summed over all cells, days and events before computing a score, so large floods weigh more (a micro-average)


basin-weighted
each river basin’s counts scaled so its flood counts once; stops one basin deciding the answer


reliability, calibration slope
whether probabilities mean what they say: of cells given P 0.6, about 60% should be flooded. Slope 1 is perfect; the target is 0.8–1.2


fold
one of five groups of events; each is scored with rates fitted on the other four


training, test (held-out) events
the first run’s one-off split: 149 events for fitting, 49 for testing


river basin
a river’s catchment, from HydroBASINS at level 4 (level 1 is a whole continent; each level splits basins into smaller sub-basins). Events in one basin stay in one fold


bootstrap interval
the range a score moves within when it is recomputed on many random re-draws of whole events; it shows how much the score depends on which events happened to be mapped


global random sample
53 blocks of 0.25° to 0.5° with no gold maps, with every day of 2023–2025 prepared: 30 random, 12 on cities and 11 reserves. The 30 blocks in Africa, Asia, South America and Oceania give the base flood rate; ordinary-day precision will be measured there


caught
a product flags at least 10% of an event’s gold-flooded floodable cells, and at least 5, on some day from 3 days before its first map to 3 days after its last. “Caught, no false event” also requires no false event


false event
the “caught” rule firing on ordinary days, when there was no mapped flood

term
meaning




STAC
a searchable catalogue of satellite files (GFM’s is at EODC)


COG
a cloud-optimised GeoTIFF: a raster file that can be read in parts over the internet


NetCDF
a file format for gridded data with several layers and a time axis; each event cube is one


blob
a file in the team’s Azure storage (dev or prod account)

text:
C.1 Reproduce from scratch
One entry per step, in order. Each gives the question, the command that reproduces it, where its outputs land, the result in one line, and the commit. Read docs/methods.md for what the numbers mean, docs/decisions.md and docs/decisions/ for why each rule was chosen, docs/final_report.md for the full write-up. Branch feat/flood-fusion-v1 (not pushed as of 2026-10-21).
Conventions used throughout: - Every rule is fixed and committed before the script that uses it runs; follow-ups that change a rule after seeing results are labelled as such. - Every number in the docs comes from a file under results/; nothing is typed by hand. - Scripts are resumable (outputs that exist are skipped) and fail loudly (a missing input raises; no event is dropped silently). - Long runs on a laptop: nice -n 19, 1–2 workers.
Inputs needed: blob credentials (DSCI_AZ_BLOB_DEV_SAS), the Earthdata token in EARTHDATA_TOKEN (MODIS and CYGNSS only), ~/.cdsapirc (snow climatology only). Everything downloads into data/fusion/ (gitignored, ~10 GB).

text:
C.2 Ledger

C.2.1 2026-10-12: v1 built end to end (phases 0–6)

Question: can a naive-Bayes fusion of GFM, FloodScan/GFDS and VIIRS beat each single product against gold?
How: make phase0 … phase6 (scripts/fusion/phase*.py); 198 events on six continents; one split, 149 fit / 49 held out, six strata, every examined cell dry before and after events.
Outputs: results/phase5_*.csv, results/accuracy_table.csv, results/prior_v1.csv, daily COGs on dev blob.
Result: held-out CSI fusion 0.285 vs VIIRS 0.319; criterion (b) fails everywhere; reliability slope ~0.01.
Commits: 07651c2 … fd0c8d6, 6b56bb6 (overstated recalibration claim corrected).



C.2.2 2026-10-13: why v1 was over-confident

D-36 agreement table (phase3_agreement.py): false alarms of different sources coincide 4–18x more than independence predicts; the gold-free table does not identify flood. 61cf986, 3350ba1.
D-39 dry-window labels (diagnostic_dry_windows.py, experiment_dry_window_fix.py): cells still flooded after the last map were labelled dry; this produced most of the over-confidence; corrected variant recall 0.37 → 0.44. 2133bd6, fc3cb9a.
D-38 seasonal mask (experiment_seasonal_baseline.py): rejected; gold counts seasonal water as flood. aba5244, a6deb13.
D-40 super-GFM (experiment_super_gfm.py): collapses to GFM persistence. 0dde253.
D-37 MODIS (experiment_modis_gold.py, modis_windows.py): fills the VIIRS archive gap (2021-01..2023-07); full-window extraction is a Databricks job blocked on an Earthdata login the job can use. 3c4ee38, 382605e, d3dd4df.
docs/methods.md written: pixels to scores. 747734a.



C.2.3 2026-10-14: the re-run design (ADRs 0003–0007)

Scope: Africa, Asia, South America, Oceania; every usable event (170). configs/fusion.yaml: scope. 2aebe4c.
Gold burn fix: burn polygon parts instead of unioning (the union took hours). 525104f. Fail-fast pools. eaa0f4f.
Five folds by HydroBASINS level-4 basin, big-flood basins placed first: events.assign_folds, make_folds.py, tests/test_folds.py. 4042ef2.
Rules fixed before any score (docs/decisions/0003–0007): three land types (snow split dropped); corrected dry-window rule adopted (gold.dry_window_rule); event-level rules (event_level in config: 10% + 5 cells, ±3 days, false-event days −30..−10). a0461a8. The unused gold.dry_day_step key removed (docs had said “every 3rd day”; code always used every day).
Cross-validation code: fusion/crossval.py, scripts/fusion/phase5_crossval.py (make crossval), tests/test_crossval.py. c97b019, 802bd33. docs/methods.md §10. 66ae80b.
Build of the 51 added events: 30 smaller ones 14 Oct; 21 large ones 14–15 Oct (laptop, restart loops; data/fusion/resume/finish_build.sh). No stage-C failures.



C.2.4 2026-10-15: the cross-validated result

make folds → results/event_folds.csv (170 events, 99 basins). One basin (four UNOSAT Bangladesh floods) holds 40% of the gold flood; its fold holds 43% of open-land flood. ADR 0004 outcome.
make crossval → results/cv/skill_*.csv, criteria.csv, reliability_*, event_level_*, f1_by_*.png. Fusion F1 0.44 (0.34–0.50) vs microwave vote 0.38, FloodScan 0.37, GFM 0.24, VIIRS 0.22; (b) passes on point estimate open/vegetated, fails urban; (c) fails. de2afda, 0292338, 361145d.
cv_breakdowns.py → skill_without_largest_basin.csv (fusion 0.35 vs 0.34 vs 0.33), skill_by_viirs_period.csv, skill_viirs_ablation.csv (VIIRS adds 0.08 F1 where it has files; without VIIRS fusion = microwave vote). ba0b8e6.
cv_normally_wet.py → normally_wet_*.csv. Normally-wet cells: 7% of labelled cells, 38% of gold flood; false-alarm rates 3–11x higher there; fusion’s lead sits there; reliability flat within both groups (slopes 0.29/0.34), so the engine, not the target, is the calibration problem. 48a7c95, 100a54d, 3daa6c5.
figure_water_vs_flood.py --count/--draw → docs/figures/water_vs_flood_cells.png, data/fusion/metrics/water_vs_flood_cells.parquet. Gold labels normally-wet cells 52% flood / 48% dry; 19% of fusion’s flood calls on gold-dry cells are there; masking them drops F1 0.44 → 0.27. 374c07e, d6aab7f.



C.2.5 2026-10-16: the cascade bar and what separates fusion from it

cv_microwave_components.py → microwave_components_*.csv. FloodScan alone costs 0.011 F1; GFDS alone 0.056; no microwave 0.106. beed811.
cv_baselines_and_views.py (rules committed first, 3850538) → baselines_views_*.csv. C.3 Open decisions and next steps (as of 2026-10-21)

Operating point: catch floods (low threshold / no memory ≈ cascade) or avoid false alarms (fusion as built or higher threshold). User’s call.
Ordinary-day precision: false-alarm rates on pre/post days cross-validated (minutes), then the global random sample with GFM as referee (sample cubes exist). Doc Next steps 6.
Normally-wet stratum (separate rates per land type × normally wet). Masks cached for map-day months; ~195 more window-months to fetch.
CYGNSS on all 148 events in coverage (~4.3 GB of windowed reads), then as a background layer (base rate) rather than daily evidence.
MODIS for the VIIRS gap: Databricks job blocked on an Earthdata login the job can use (user’s consent for a personal token as a secret, or the team account fixed).
FloodScan licence outside Africa unconfirmed; GFDS feed ended 2026-09-14.
Water-first redesign (fuse water, subtract one normal-water baseline): a target-clarity change, not a calibration fix.
